User wants help writing a comprehensive content plan about NCAT (#NCAT), built from information the user supplies from the NCAT website. The target persona/audience for the content is homeowners (#content-plan-homeowners).

#NCAT overview: the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) decides a range of civil and administrative cases in New South Wales. It commenced on 1 January 2014, consolidating 22 former tribunals into a single point of access for specialist tribunal services. It is established and governed by the Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 2013.

#NCAT Consumer and Commercial Division resolves a wide range of everyday disputes such as tenancy and other residential disputes, and consumer claims. Its housing and property case types are: tenancy, social housing, boarding houses, residential communities, holiday parks, agricultural tenancy, strata schemes, community schemes, home building, retirement villages, and dividing fences.

#NCAT Consumer and Commercial Division consumer/business case types: consumer claims, motor vehicles, retail leases, agent commissions and fees, conveyancing costs, pawnbrokers and second-hand dealers.

#NCAT Appeal Panel determines internal appeals from decisions of NCAT's Divisions where a right of appeal to the Appeal Panel is provided under the Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 2013 (NCAT Act) or enabling legislation. It also hears designated external appeals under the NCAT Act or enabling legislation. Before appealing or seeking leave to appeal, parties should read the NCAT Guideline on Internal Appeals and learn about making an internal appeal.

#NCAT application process: you can apply to NCAT to make certain decisions, review decisions or resolve a dispute; NCAT deals with everyday issues such as tenancy and building works disputes, guardianship decisions and administrative review of government decisions. The process varies by case type and time limits may apply — select the case type that best describes the dispute.

#NCAT applying: to start proceedings you complete an application form and lodge it with the appropriate fee; all forms are downloadable in PDF-fillable format and some application types can be lodged online. The application must give your name and contact details, the other party's name and contact details, the orders you want NCAT to make, and the reasons for those orders. Urgent issues have a separate urgent hearing process.

#NCAT fees and time limits: an application fee may be payable depending on case type, with a reduced concession fee for eligible persons (see NCAT fees and charges); time limits may also apply and should be checked in the information for the relevant case type.

#NCAT applying against a business or company: you must provide the name of the individual or company that owns the business, the registered name and address, and their ABN or ACN, plus a business name or company extract. If the other party is a permanent resident of another State, the application may be affected by federal jurisdiction.

#NCAT offers a simple, quick and effective process for resolving disputes and reviewing administrative action, including support for self-representation in most matters, plain language forms and documents, simplified processes, and a range of alternative dispute resolution methods.

#NCAT case types are broad and diverse — from tenancy issues and building works to guardianship decisions and administrative review of government decisions — and are generally managed through its Divisions, with the Appeal Panel providing timely, cost-effective review of most Tribunal decisions.

#NCAT "How NCAT works" steps: (1) Application process — identify your case type, then complete an application form; (2) Prepare for your hearing once NCAT sends a notice of hearing; (3) Resolve a case by agreement, using NCAT's alternative resolution processes before the hearing; (4) On the hearing day, know what to expect on arrival; (5) After the hearing, NCAT makes a decision and orders; (6) Appeal an NCAT decision — certain decisions can be internally appealed to the Appeal Panel.
#NCAT jurisdiction and diverse case types are generally managed through its four Divisions and the Appeal Panel.

#NCAT Appeal Panel: it determines internal appeals from decisions made by NCAT's Divisions, where a right of appeal is provided under the Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act 2013 (NCAT Act) or enabling legislation, and also hears designated external appeals.
#NCAT guidance for appeals: before proceeding with an appeal or asking for leave to appeal, read the NCAT Guideline on Internal Appeals and learn about making an internal appeal.

In the well-known Australian bat lyssavirus case discussed on 2023/05/28, the woman died about two and a half years after her encounter with the bat; where on her body she was bitten/scratched and the autopsy findings were not publicly reported. #lyssavirus #australia #bat-lyssavirus

Correction noted on 2023/05/28: an earlier claim that "50% of flying foxes carry bat lyssavirus" was wrong; prevalence varies widely by species and location (e.g. up to ~30% in some black flying fox populations, far lower elsewhere) and human transmission is rare. #lyssavirus #fact-check

Kuru facts: prion disease of the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, spread by mortuary cannibalism (brain, lungs, intestines eaten); most prevalent in the 1950s-60s, killing roughly 10% of the population; long incubation (years) then progressive tremors, ataxia and dementia, fatal within about a year of onset; it declined sharply after the practice stopped and no new cases since the 1990s. #kuru #prion #papua-new-guinea
